readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
It is the Lord who speaks:
I am going to lure her
and lead her out into the wilderness
and speak to her heart.
There she will respond to me as she did when she was young,
as she did when she came out of the land of Egypt.
When that day comes – it is the Lord who speaks –
she will call me, ‘My husband’,
no longer will she call me, ‘My Baal.’
I will betroth you to myself for ever,
betroth you with integrity and justice,
with tenderness and love;
I will betroth you to myself with faithfulness,
and you will come to know the Lord.

exegesis.summary: Through the prophet Hosea, God unveils the astonishing tenderness of his covenant: he will lure unfaithful Israel into the wilderness to speak to her heart and betroth her to himself forever in integrity, justice, tenderness, love, and faithfulness. The idolatry that made Israel call God 'my Baal' (my master) will give way to the intimate cry 'my husband.' This is the language of spousal love, revealing that the Lord's covenant is nothing less than a marriage.

patristicQuotes.quote: The Lord speaks, if we may say it, as a lover would to his mistress who despised him, and was therefore about to be punished.

cccReferences.title: God calls man first to the covenant of prayer
God merciful and faithful despite Israel's sin
The Bride betrothed to the Bridegroom

exegesis.thematicConnection: Hosea's promise of a Bridegroom who heals and restores his beloved prepares us for the Gospel, where Jesus, the divine Bridegroom in the flesh, reaches out to heal a bleeding woman and raise a dead daughter — the concrete signs of the betrothal Hosea foretold.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
The Lord is kind and full of compassion.
I will bless you day after day
and praise your name for ever.
The Lord is great, highly to be praised,
his greatness cannot be measured.
The Lord is kind and full of compassion.
Age to age shall proclaim your works,
shall declare your mighty deeds,
shall speak of your splendour and glory,
tell the tale of your wonderful works.
The Lord is kind and full of compassion.
They will speak of your terrible deeds,
recount your greatness and might.
They will recall your abundant goodness;
age to age shall ring out your justice.
The Lord is kind and full of compassion.
The Lord is kind and full of compassion,
slow to anger, abounding in love.
How good is the Lord to all,
compassionate to all his creatures.
The Lord is kind and full of compassion.
readings.refrain: The Lord is kind and full of compassion.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist blesses the Lord day after day, proclaiming his greatness that cannot be measured and his tender compassion that reaches every creature. The refrain — 'The Lord is kind and full of compassion' — echoes God's self-revelation to Moses as 'slow to anger, abounding in love.' Praise here is not a bargain but the spontaneous joy of a heart that has tasted mercy.

patristicQuotes.quote: Consider what a blessed privilege is granted thee, to talk with God in thy prayers, and make known to Him all thy wants, while He, though not in words, yet by His mercy, answers thee; for He despiseth not petitions, He tires not, but when thou art silent.

cccReferences.title: Prayer of praise given for God's own sake
Our heart is restless until it rests in God

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm gives voice to the response Hosea foresaw — the Bride learning to praise her Bridegroom — and it names the very attribute (compassion) that Jesus displays in the Gospel toward the hemorrhaging woman and the grieving father.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: While Jesus was speaking, up came one of the officials, who bowed low in front of him and said, ‘My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her and her life will be saved.’ Jesus rose and, with his disciples, followed him. Then from behind him came a woman, who had suffered from a haemorrhage for twelve years, and she touched the fringe of his cloak, for she said to herself, ‘If I can only touch his cloak I shall be well again.’ Jesus turned round and saw her; and he said to her, ‘Courage, my daughter, your faith has restored you to health.’ And from that moment the woman was well again.

exegesis.summary: Two desperate people — a synagogue official whose daughter has just died and a woman bleeding for twelve years — approach Jesus with faith, and both receive life. The woman touches only the fringe of his cloak in silent hope; Jesus turns, calls her 'daughter,' and heals her. He then enters the ruler's house and raises the girl from death. The Bridegroom of Hosea now walks among his people, healing and restoring life by touch and word.

patristicQuotes.quote: How wonderful her faith, that though she despaired of health from the physicians, on whom she had exhausted her living, she perceived that a heavenly Physician was at hand, and therefore bent her whole soul on Him; whence she deserved to be healed.

Christ would not suffer her to go away unobserved... He relieves the woman's fear, He corrects her error in supposing she could be hid from Him, He displays her faith to all for their imitation, and He shews He knew all things, no less than in drying the fountain of her blood.

cccReferences.title: Christ the physician of body and soul
Love as the source of prayer that does not disappoint

exegesis.thematicConnection: The healings enact Hosea's promise in the flesh: Jesus 'speaks to the heart' of the trembling woman, calling her 'daughter,' and He touches death itself to restore a child to life. Faith is the response of the Bride who reaches out for her Lord.

synthesis.title: The Bridegroom Who Speaks to the Heart
synthesis.body: Today the Church invites us into the wedding language of God. Hosea reveals a Lord who does not tire of unfaithful Israel but leads her back into the wilderness to woo her: 'I will betroth you to myself for ever, with integrity and justice, with tenderness and love.' This is the astonishing shape of the covenant — a marriage, not a transaction. The psalm gives the Bride's answering song: 'The Lord is kind and full of compassion,' the very words with which God once revealed his name to Moses. Then, in the Gospel, the Bridegroom steps out of prophecy and walks the roads of Galilee. A woman worn out by twelve years of bleeding stretches out in silent faith and touches only the tassel of his cloak; a father whose daughter lies dead begs him to come and lay his hand on her. To both, Jesus gives life. He turns to the woman and calls her 'daughter' — the intimate name Hosea promised. He takes the girl by the hand and death releases her. What Hosea foretold in poetry, Christ accomplishes in flesh: God has come to speak to the heart of his people, to heal what no physician could heal, and to raise what only love can raise. Our part today is the woman's part — to reach out, however tremblingly, and touch him.
